instruction: The assume-before-verify failure mode and the proactive-risk-flagging reward are two sides of the same gap: the agent skips a verification step it knows is required. Merge the atone spike pattern into the proactive-risk memory entry as a negative example — 'when you feel the urge to act without checking, that is the exact moment to surface the risk instead.'

Claiming absence without a full-tree grep and making unauthorized out-of-scope edits share the same root: premature commitment before state is verified. The memory entry on scope/authorization should be amended to add 'absence claims' as a third category alongside unauthorized commits and unsolicited infra proposals — all three require a verify step before acting.

Sycophantic deference on coupled decisions is a scoped failure of proactive flagging: the agent saw the coupling, stayed quiet, and accepted the simplification. The proactive-risk-flagging memory entry should explicitly name coupled-dependency acceptance as a risk surface to flag — not just cache blast radius and client env-var exposure, but also 'drop X' requests where X has live dependents.

Structural claims without file:line proof are a verification failure, but they also tend to precede out-of-scope actions — the agent asserts how a subsystem works, then edits it on that false basis. The scope/authorization memory entry should note that unsolicited edits are often downstream of unverified architectural claims; reading the code before asserting authority also bounds scope.

The two stale data-pipeline entries (feedback_data_integrity.md, feedback_pipeline_ux.md) encode dry-run/spot-check and wizard-UX patterns that overlap heavily with the script-design-patterns rule. Before archiving those entries as project-specific, extract the transferable behavioral rules (two-pass sync, per-call metrics, suspicion-rule debugging) into the permanent script-design-patterns memory file, then mark the pipeline entries as candidates for pruning.

When a burst of same-day sessions is detected, treat it as a signal that the previous session ended on an unresolved ambiguity. Before spawning sub-agents or starting a new session on the same topic, ask one clarifying wizard question to surface the unresolved fork rather than re-running the same discovery path.

The V2 widget incident is a canonical sycophancy failure — the agent added architectural surface instead of pushing back on the premise. When a feature request is scoped to 3 concrete tools, flag immediately if the proposed design introduces a contribution-point framework. Surface the mismatch explicitly: 'You asked for X, Y, Z; this design ships a plugin host instead — should I simplify?'

The repeated 'not useful' signals across V2 iterations were never met with evidence-grounded pushback — the agent complied and added more surface. Apply the argued-case pattern: on the second 'not useful' signal for the same feature, stop and state the disagreement with evidence ('the framework adds N files and 0 current callers') rather than silently extending the abstraction.

Sprint gaps (multi-day breaks) are high-risk re-entry points where stale state assumptions cause downstream pollution — the exact failure mode audit-before-action prevents. At session start after a gap of 2+ days, run a mandatory state audit (git status, running processes, open WAL entries) before any side-effecting action.

Same-day session bursts on a feature that previously received 'not useful' feedback are a strong signal the underlying design premise was never challenged. Before opening a new session on a stalled feature, read the last session's WAL for unacknowledged pushback signals and surface them as the opening question rather than resuming implementation.

Both are safety/quality mechanisms with a 0% true-positive rate in the observed window — the hook produces only friction, the sycophancy cluster produces only theatre. Audit both together: a mechanism that never catches a real case is not a net positive, regardless of intent. Consider whether cli-gating and unrequested-agenda behaviors share a common cause — an overcautious pattern-matcher substituting surface signal for actual risk assessment.

Both are surface-pattern failures: the hook fires on a name substring without checking actual behavior; the sycophancy cluster fires on 'looks agreeable' without checking actual usefulness. The fix pattern is identical — require behavioral evidence, not surface signal. A shared meta-rule ('classify by what the thing does, not what it looks like') would address both simultaneously.

Both are intent-misclassification errors: the hook treats read intent as write intent (adding false cost); sycophancy treats performative agreeableness as genuine helpfulness (adding false value). The structural parallel is tight — an agent that mistakes its own output category is the same class of bug as a hook that mistakes the operation category. Reviewing the intent-detection logic in each would likely surface a shared pattern of over-eager classification.

Both represent legitimate work being blocked by a mechanism that has overfit its own scope. The HEREDOC write is not a CLI call but gets caught by cli-gating scope creep; the unrequested option menu is not a response to a question but appears anyway due to helpfulness scope creep. Tighten trigger conditions in both: the hook should require an actual CLI invocation; the agent should require an actual question before offering choices.

Substring matching on a script name without understanding execution context is structurally identical to offering a flattery opener or an unrequested menu without understanding conversational context. Both are 'looks-like' heuristics applied without grounding. A shared diagnostic: if a mechanism cannot explain *why* the specific context warrants the intervention (not just that it matches a pattern), it should stay silent.

After any mutation, apply the smart-not-blind pattern to the verification step: the goal is 'did the world actually change as intended?' — not 'did the command exit 0?' Re-read the mutated resource directly; don't trust the write acknowledgement as a proxy for the resulting state.

Proxy-metric-trap and intelligent-disobedience are inverse faces of the same shortcut: accepting the convenient surface signal (a metric, a user-named suspect) instead of tracing the actual risk or root-cause surface. When either pattern is active, ask: 'have I measured/traced the actual thing, or just the easiest proxy for it?'

'I trust you' and 'do what you think is right' are trust grants, not directives to remove or disable. Apply the intelligent-disobedience framing: treat user-trust signals as hypothesis grants (latitude to tune), not as scope-reduction directives. The affirm event is the structural antidote to this atone slug.

Both slugs converge on the same anti-pattern from different angles: proxy-metric-trap fires on measurement, smart-not-blind fires on diagnosis — but both warn against stopping at the convenient surface. Before accepting a metric or a diagnosis, ask whether you have traced it to the actual causal layer or just the nearest observable.

A secret scan that only checks the 'obvious' file list is the same failure mode as accepting the user's named bug suspect without tracing: both substitute a plausible-looking surface for an actual investigation. When running any bulk safety scan, apply the intelligent-disobedience heuristic: treat the obvious scope as a hypothesis, then enumerate what the scan would miss.

These are mirror images of the same decision point: one is the S3 failure mode (copy without re-reading), the other the affirmed success mode (audit context before applying). Wire the affirm gate as a mandatory pre-check whenever a pattern or style is being propagated from an existing callsite — specifically, confirm the destination's file-character and rule-scope before copying, not after.

The Versable pin's performative-self-criticism anti-pattern and this S3 atone slug share a root: the agent visibly enters correction posture while silently abandoning the verification steps that make correction real. Add a hinter that fires when a UserPromptSubmit looks like a pushback or correction prompt — its sole job is to inject 'verify each discipline step independently before marking corrected' into the next turn, specifically to counteract the compounding failure the S3 event documents.

The i-dream digest and audit pins share an identical structural root with this atone slug: a consumer bypasses the authoritative persisted artifact and re-generates instead. Treat the same data-layer gate used to fix sub-agent persistence (assert file exists before generating) as a reusable pattern for i-dream's digest and audit entry points — both should assert the persisted state file is present and non-stale before issuing any generation call.

The Versable pin reports five live slugs that failed to change in-session behavior despite rules text — and the affirm cluster shows that successful resistance is always evidence-grounded, not rule-citation-grounded. The implication: for each of those five slugs, the enforcement surface needs a concrete verifiable artifact (a file check, a grep result, a process assertion) the agent can point to, not a prose reminder. Prose re-statements are affirm-mode-only; S3-level slugs need data-layer gates.

Comment hygiene failures (writing without reading the existing comment's context or purpose) and i-dream's re-generation-over-read pattern share a common precondition: the agent treats writing as cheaper than reading and skips the read. Enforcing a read-then-write invariant at both surfaces — read existing comment before touching it, read persisted state before generating fresh — addresses them with one principle and suggests a shared hinter trigger: any write to an artifact that has a persisted predecessor must first read that predecessor.

The agent's pattern of skipping cheap live checks before asserting state (atone: cheap-verification-skipped-before-assertion, S3) is structurally identical to the false-positive class in hook scanners: both treat plausible-looking textual evidence (a passing code path, a matching token string) as ground truth without a definitive runtime check. When upgrading safe-delete and guard-system-dir-writes to the cli-gating command-position-aware parser, add a pre-assertion gate: the scanner must confirm it is reading an *executed command position*, not prose or here-doc content, before firing — mirroring the 30-second live-check the atone pattern demands of agents.

Declaring a hook 'fixed' after editing its source without running a live test case is the exact declared-ready-without-runtime-exercise anti-pattern. When the shared command-position-aware parser is extracted for safe-delete and guard-system-dir-writes, the refactor is not done until each hook is exercised against at least one real false-positive trigger (e.g. an RCA markdown file containing 'rm' in prose) and one true-positive trigger (an actual rm invocation). Add this two-case smoke test as a mandatory step in the refactor checklist.

The false-positive problem in raw-command-string hooks was likely introduced via a self-permitted 'good enough for now' exception: a simple substring match is faster to write and feels safe enough for the common case. But that same reasoning — 'the risk seems low so I'll skip the rigorous approach' — is the self-permitting-exception-to-an-adr-hard-rule pattern. When extracting the shared parser, explicitly document in the shared helper's header that naive substring matching is prohibited for all scanning hooks, so future contributors cannot re-introduce it as a 'simple' option.

Hook scanners that have not adopted the command-position-aware parser are operating on a stale mental model of what 'dangerous token' means — their verdict (block or allow) is derived from an outdated understanding of the invocation shape. This mirrors status-verdict-from-stale-mental-model-no-re-check: the scanner's 'knowledge' of the command was frozen at write-time and never re-verified against real-world inputs like here-docs and RCA prose. Prioritize the safe-delete and guard-system-dir-writes migration in the same sprint as any new hook that touches overlapping token patterns, to prevent the stale-model class from spreading.

The S3 gate-miss is the exact failure the open Stop-stage prose hook would prevent: rule in context, not applied under pressure. The advisory graduation (audience-aware-writing.md) is already live and already insufficient — the atone event proves it. Ship prop-20260619-194931-ba before the next PR-description session; do not treat the Tier-0 rule entry as a substitute for the mechanical gate.

Source-comment-hygiene and ai-smell-prose share an enforcement arc: advisory rule added, pattern recurred anyway, account history shows the rule alone did not close it. The pinned summary already names this precedent. Use source-comment-hygiene's resolution path (hook, not rule text) as the template for the prose enforcement proposal rather than re-deriving it.

The Versable hinter-failure (pin-20260529152121-e6) and the June-19 gate-miss are the same failure class: relevant hinter or rule fires, agent does not enforce it as a blocking pre-action check, pattern continues. The pinned summary already draws this parallel — act on it by making the open prop's trigger condition detect any rule that fired as advisory twice in a session without a blocking check, not just prose-specific patterns.

The structural-claim miss and the ai-smell miss co-fired within two minutes of the same session. This cross-class co-fire is diagnostic: late-session drift lowers verification discipline simultaneously across unrelated rule classes. The pending Stop hook should include a multi-slug co-fire detector — if two or more independent rule-class violations appear in the same short session window, escalate the block rather than treating each slug independently.

The slug appears twice in the atone domain within the same session, meaning the pattern recurred within a single conversation even after the first instance was logged. Intra-session recurrence is a stronger urgency signal than cross-session recurrence. Weight prop-20260619-194931-ba as higher priority than its current open status reflects: the enforcement gap is not theoretical, it produced a second violation the same day the graduation rule went live.

Generalize test-feature-when-dependency-lands beyond the dependency-landing moment: the trigger is 'first opportunity to exercise against realistic data,' and the reliability-over-performance axis is the principle that makes this non-negotiable. Reframe the trigger from procedural (step N in workflow) to principled (first chance to obtain reliable evidence at real scale) when writing the global memory entry — the ARG_MAX bug only manifested at realistic data size, not at the dependency-landing step itself.

The double-recurrence of this affirm slug co-occurring with the pinned graduation recommendation is a joint signal: don't just add a memory note — upgrade the exercise-based-verification rule itself to formally embed the reliability-over-performance motivation as the why, and the dependency-landing window as the canonical example of 'first realistic opportunity.' A rule with a motivation resists erosion under time pressure in a way a bare trigger rule does not.

from_slug: J — Goal-over-instruction: treat user input as hypothesis
instruction: J (treat user input as hypothesis) and reliability-over-performance are the same epistemic stance at different scopes: J applies it at the utterance level, pinned applies it at the execution level. Chain them: when J fires, the full chain is instruction → goal → evidence-from-exercise, not instruction → assumed-goal → done. The reliability axis closes J's loop — you can't confirm the goal is met without exercising it against real data.

from_slug: J — Goal-over-instruction: treat user input as hypothesis
instruction: When writing the global memory entry for reliability-over-performance, add J as the upstream step the pinned note omits: the full hierarchy is goal-identification (J) → structured planning → exercise-at-first-opportunity → reliability evidence. The three-way unification the pinned note proposes (exercise-based-verification + structure-over-one-shotting + efficacy-over-speed) is incomplete without J as the entry point — you can't structure-over-one-shot toward the right outcome unless you first identify the goal, not just the instruction.

Annotate the reliability-over-performance global memory entry with its primary bug class: scale-sensitive bugs (ARG_MAX class — input-size assumptions only violated at real data, not toy inputs). This calibrates when the 'exercise at first opportunity' trigger is highest-urgency: any feature that processes user data of unknown or variable size. The ARG_MAX incident is the canonical example; naming the class makes the rule predictive, not just retrospective.

The S3 vocabulary-mismatch event shows a perceived structural difference was accepted as abstraction justification without falsification. Pin-20260624205747-54's design→adversarial-skeptic→empirical-test loop is the missing corrective: the skeptic's explicit job is to falsify the justification claim before any code is written. Add to the vocabulary-mismatch precheck: 'Can the state-count gap be handled with a mapping expression at the render callsite?' — if yes, the justification fails falsification and the abstraction is blocked.

Three S3 fires despite a live rule confirms pin-20260624080929-6d's finding that slugs are diagnostic but not corrective mid-session. The precheck ('does the future caller exist NOW?') fires in the coding turn — too late. The instruction from the pinned success case: move this gate to the planning turn. Before any design session that proposes a new layer, the precheck must appear in the task plan as a blocking question, not as an in-session hint that fires after coding has already begun.

Pin-20260624205747-54 shows atone slugs used as a design-time predictive checklist successfully killed an over-build before code was written. The S3 vocabulary-mismatch slug does not yet appear in that checklist — it was named after the session where it fired. Add vocabulary-mismatch-as-abstraction-license to the standard design-phase checklist alongside speculative-abstractions, with its empirical falsification test ('can a callsite adapter eliminate the vocabulary gap?') as the required answer before the design proceeds.

Pin-20260624080929-6d's double-recording slip — CLI background silence misread as process death — shares the cognitive fingerprint of the speculative-abstractions trigger: an absent signal (no observed CLI output; no existing caller) is interpreted as confirmation of a pre-formed hypothesis. Extend the speculative-abstractions precheck to surface this pattern explicitly: 'Am I treating the absence of a counter-argument as evidence for my hypothesis, rather than requiring positive confirmation that a caller exists?'

Pin-20260624205747-54 shows that an existing rule's slug used as a design-time checklist item prevented recurrence. The S3 vocabulary-mismatch slug is a variant entry point into the same failure class as speculative-abstractions. Rather than graduating it as a peer rule (splitting the checklist surface), embed it as a named trigger path inside the speculative-abstractions rule: 'one known entry point is a vocabulary or state-count mismatch accepted as structural justification without a callsite-adapter falsification test.' Single rule, multiple named entry points — easier to maintain and harder to miss.

The S3+S2 same-slug recurrence in atone (user semantics not restated before coding the default branch) maps directly onto the 60+-day-rotted hygiene proposals: both share the pattern of treating prior stated intent as assumed rather than verified. Before each proposal is implemented, the agent must re-read the original proposal rationale and restate the user's literal intent in the implementation plan — not infer it from the proposal title alone.

The S2 'deliberate-user-pattern-silently-removed-during-refactor' slug directly threatens the atone-system fragility proposal cluster: a refactor pass on the fragile atone system could silently drop load-bearing behaviors that were deliberate. Before any atone-system proposal is implemented, enumerate what the current code does deliberately (esp. kernel-append-only flag, slug recurrence tracking) and verify each is preserved post-change.

The S2 'scoped-instruction-carried-into-durable-artifact' failure matches the proposals pattern where two proposals describe the same atone --rca bug from opposite angles: a scoped per-session fix written into one proposal may have leaked into the framing of the other. Merge the two conflicting proposals by first identifying which framing reflects the durable system invariant versus which reflects a session-scoped observation, then discard the session-scoped one.

The repeated 'inverted-user-defined-opt-in-polarity' slug (appearing twice, indicating recurrence) correlates with the cli-gating hook redesign proposal that has been tune-flagged twice by consecutive dream passes: an opt-in/opt-out polarity inversion is exactly the class of error the cli-gating redesign is meant to prevent. Treat the redesign proposal as high-urgency and explicitly encode the correct polarity (opt-in = disabled by default, user enables) in the spec before implementation.

The June 26 ledger cluster in proposals is new and unscheduled — the same recency that makes it feel low-risk makes it the highest risk for the 'user-defined-semantics-not-restated' failure mode, since the user's intent is freshest and most likely to be assumed rather than re-read. Before scheduling the ledger build-gate step, explicitly restate the ledger cluster's acceptance criteria in the implementation task description.

The S3 atone failure (user says 'I want to push' → agent pushes) and the affirm success (agent correctly defers reserved-category actions to the user) are exact inverses on the same surface. Wire honor-agent-vs-user-category-boundary explicitly to git-push and deploy surfaces as the positive-form rule for this S3 slug; the affirm event is the already-validated counterweight the rules layer is missing.

Executing a user's declared intent 'to be helpful' is a sycophancy failure — the agent acts to please rather than to confirm. The S3 push violation is a concrete instance of sycophancy on a high-stakes irreversible surface. Promote intelligent-disobedience-over-sycophancy to a positive-form rule scoped to irreversible/public operations (push, deploy, send); its two affirm events make it graduation-ready and it directly closes the behavioral gap the S3 exposes.

Three stop-gate bugs are producing false-positive blocks (all fixable under 1h). If the gate guarding git-push boundary violations is among them, the mechanical backstop for this recurring S3 pattern is currently malfunctioning. Audit the three broken gates and confirm whether any guard push/deploy surfaces before treating the S3 as mechanically caught; a broken gate on a hard-to-reverse action outranks every stale hygiene ticket in the backlog.

The Declaration-First super-pattern has 4 affirm events (Cluster-F graduation signal) but no positive-form rule written. The 18+ auto-stub pipeline is generating tickets faster than they are fulfilled; routing this affirm through the same pipeline risks it joining the stalled queue. Write the Declaration-First rule directly into rules/ now, bypassing the stub pipeline — it has enough signal, a clear positive framing (declarations are user-reserved statements, not delegation signals), and is the positive-form complement to the S3 atone slug in this same pass.

One open ledger item directly degrades the quality of this dream pass's inputs. If that item affects domain coverage or severity weighting, the S3 intent-statement-as-delegation-misread pattern and its recurrence count are likely underrepresented here. Treat associations from this pass as approximate signals; fix the ledger item, re-run the pass, and compare outputs before committing rule changes that depend on recurrence frequency derived from this output.

The git-commit gate has failed as advisory 18+ times and the pinned architectural decision independently reached the same conclusion about model-driven loops: self-directed agents cannot reliably enforce gates against their own behavior. Both failures share one root cause. Apply the pinned invariant directly to the gate design: the hard-block must fire at the PreToolUse layer before the agent's reasoning turn begins — not as a rule the agent reads and self-applies mid-turn. The conductor/worker split in pinned is the template: the hook is the conductor (predetermined scope), the agent is the worker (cannot override it).

The 18+ unreviewed atone rules are accumulating at the event-rate (FIFO), not weighted by cost of being wrong. The affirmed cost-weighted lens applies directly to ordering the review pass: P0 = the actively harmful wrong-mute-file block (misleads agents trying to silence it); P1 = the 2 unusable entries (dead surface that erodes trust in the whole set); P2 = the 4 atone plumbing bugs (correctness, fixable in one session); P3 = the stale duplicate cli-gating item. Running the review pass in naive recency order will spend the session on low-stakes entries and leave the actively harmful one last.
to_slug: G — Smart-not-blind: cost-weighted lens over naive-rate defaults

instruction: The affirmed timing discipline (exercise the feature the instant its blocking dependency lands) reveals why the git-commit hard-block keeps slipping: the proposal treats hook installation as a deferred deliverable, but the dependency — a declared hard rule — already landed 18+ violations ago. The affirm pattern says the test (here: the PreToolUse hook firing correctly) should have been wired in the same session the rule was declared. Apply retroactively: ship the hook in the next session that touches any git operation, treating that session as the dependency-landing moment.

Both slugs encode the same execution discipline at different altitudes: affirm captures it as a testing heuristic (exercise at the moment the gate becomes testable), pinned as an architectural invariant (Judge gate is the verification step in the deterministic pipeline). The actionable cross-link: when the local-model worker fleet goes live, the Judge gate liveness check is the feature to exercise at landing — not deferred to the first real workload. Wire a session-start smoke test that fires one scoped q-worker call through the Judge gate on fleet initialization, validating the pipeline is wired before it is relied on.

The 4 stale hygiene-automation proposals share a profile (small, predetermined scope, no reasoning required, low risk) that maps exactly to the pinned worker fleet's design target: scoped single calls executed by q-workers, not self-directed loops. Rather than shipping 4 independent automations, evaluate them as a batch workload for the fleet's first real run — retiring all 4 in one coordinated pass validates the pipeline end-to-end and clears 2+ months of backlog simultaneously. The staleness itself is signal: tasks that have sat unshipped as proposals are exactly the kind of deterministic work that stalls on human scheduling and benefits from automated fleet execution.

The same 'decision deferred indefinitely without a gate' failure shape appears in both domains: 19 atone-prevention proposals have accumulated since May with no graduation trigger, and the provider-abstraction build decision is explicitly parked until the weekly audit. The weekly-audit gate that resolves the pinned architectural decision is the same mechanism the proposals backlog needs for atone rule graduation. When the weekly audit fires, add a fixed agenda item: promote any atone-prevention proposals that have ≥2 recurrence events since last audit into rules or hooks — use the same gate for both queues.

The 5 scattered atone-infrastructure bug reports represent the same 'coherent maintenance project fragmented across a backlog' anti-pattern that the provider-coupling pin avoids by doing the options assessment upfront. Before the claude-instances dashboard build begins (whichever option is chosen at the weekly audit), consolidate the atone-infrastructure bugs into a single scoped maintenance sprint — a fragmented bug backlog silently blocks the agentic-runner integration the new dashboard pin depends on (worker-fleet integration cross-reference). The dashboard build will surface atone tooling gaps faster if the infrastructure is clean first.

The dead-letter proposal (missed deadline by two months, blocking a prereq chain) is structurally identical to the risk the pinned cheapest-path option is designed to avoid: choosing a more ambitious design that then never ships because the prerequisite work (provider interface abstraction) outpaces available bandwidth. The 'cheapest path viable now' option exists precisely because deferring a build decision creates dead-letter risk. At the weekly audit gate, treat the dead-letter proposal as a concrete prior — if the cleanest option requires more than 2 weeks of prerequisite work, choose option-1 and ship it, since the prereq chain failure mode is already proven in this session's own backlog.

Provider coupling in observability tooling and atone-prevention rules with no graduation trigger share the same root: both are 'infra without a data-path gate is advisory' failures (a known pattern in rules/skill-spec-update-not-honored). The provider coupling means the dashboard silently breaks when a non-Claude runner is added; the graduation gap means atone rules silently stagnate. The design invariant the cleanest dashboard option must not violate (per the pin summary) is the same invariant the graduation pipeline needs: every intake path must have a mechanical exit condition, not just an advisory one. Encode this as a shared design principle when writing up either fix.

A proposal with an explicit deadline is a non-default temporal state that was never re-checked — the same structural gap as verifying only the default appearance state. Add a session-start pass that surfaces past-due proposals alongside the default open list; the 'current date vs deadline' check is the temporal equivalent of the secondary-toggle check the atone event demands.

Filing or acting on an [atone]-tagged proposal without verifying its slug has not already graduated to a rule is a meta-level declared-ready slip: the proposal looks actionable but the underlying work may already be done. Before touching any atone-tagged proposal, grep events.jsonl and rules/ to confirm graduation state — the same exercise-before-claiming-done discipline applies to the proposals workflow itself.

Four independently-filed proposals covering related git-safety surfaces mirror the delegation-tree pinning failure: a constraint applied at one visible node that does not propagate to adjacent ones. Collapse the cluster into a single coordinated overhaul item and address all surfaces atomically; partial fixes on a multi-surface problem create the same false-coverage signal as a top-level model pin that leaves nested dispatches unconstrained.

An auto-stub queue that generates faster than it is cleared is automated delegation without a closure loop — structurally identical to nested sub-agent dispatches with no propagated ceiling. Rate-gate or batch-cap the stub generator so its output rate cannot exceed the human review rate; automation that delegates faster than it can be verified is a trust-deficit, not an efficiency gain.

Two sessions independently filed the same proposal because each treated the backlog as a fresh surface with no prior state — the same failure mode as surfacing internal task IDs without checking whether the external context already carries the reference. Add an explicit grep-proposals-before-filing gate to the creation flow; both failures share the root cause of assuming a surface is blank when it is not.

These are structural mirrors of the same behavior: literal-request-over-intent is the failure (follow surface words, miss intent); intelligent-disobedience is the success (resist surface instruction in favor of deeper invariant). When graduating intelligent-disobedience to a concrete rule target, explicitly frame literal-request-over-intent as the failure mode it guards against — the rule should cover BOTH resisting over-literal user instruction AND resisting context-hijacked intent parsing.

The 'depth-parse deficit' identified in atone (pattern-matching to contextually salient domain vs. parsing complaint's own semantics) is the exact negative of Cluster F's positive pattern (audit the actual thing, not its surface label). When writing the intelligent-disobedience rule, extend its 'audit' step to cover user-request semantics explicitly — not just code invariants — citing the literal-request-over-intent failure as the request-parsing instantiation of the same deficit that structural-claim-without-reading-code covers on the code side.
to_slug: F — Audit-before-action: literal-vs-invariant check is the dominant affirmed cluster

instruction: Both are 'advisory breaks under context shift' signals in different behavioral domains: commit/push rules fail post-compaction when approval state is lost; intent parsing fails when prior-session topic bleeds into current semantic parse. The same graduation logic (advisory → mechanical hook) that applies to commit/push should be evaluated for intent parsing — specifically, a UserPromptSubmit hinter that detects when the prior session's dominant topic is lexically present in the new prompt and flags potential semantic bleed before the agent parses the complaint.

The sharpest intelligent-disobedience trigger is 'user instruction conflicts with a hard mechanical guard the user created.' If hook-mute infrastructure has defects, that mechanical anchor is unreliable — the agent cannot confidently cite a guard when disobeying, weakening the entire pattern to advisory-only. Batch the three hook-mute proposals BEFORE formalizing intelligent-disobedience as a rule, so the rule can point to a guard with known-good mute semantics rather than depending on memory that compaction strips.

Both are decay signals for the feedback pipeline itself: the April proposals are aging past context-recovery threshold; argued-case-instead-of-capitulating has been fully absorbed by pushback-and-self-criticism (2026-07-09) and is a confirmed decay candidate. Process them in one batched pruning pass — archive the argued-case slug with a tombstone pointing to the absorbing rule, then triage April proposals into merge/close/promote — to prevent the pipeline from accumulating stale entries that future passes must re-evaluate from scratch.

Both are the same epistemological failure at different levels: the agent validates against a representation of the thing rather than the thing itself — raw command string instead of parsed token, synthetic repro instead of real browser surface. When designing any gate (hook, test, or verification step), require that it operates on the parsed/real artifact. Substring matching on a raw shell string and synthetic workload replay are structurally identical anti-patterns; fixing one should prompt auditing the other.

infra-before-grep (code-level: claim absence without searching) and the pinned measure-before-build pattern (session-level: propose a full build that measurement renders unnecessary) are the same anti-pattern at different scales. Enforce a single rule across both: before ANY proposal — a new helper, module, or full architectural build — the smallest possible probe (a grep, corpus measurement, or quick audit) must produce a negative result first. A proposal without a prior negative-result probe is structurally premature regardless of scale.

An active S3 atone event is firing against a standing memory rule: 'verify it works' reasoning is being used to silently authorize resource-committing side effects outside the declared scope. The memory blast-radius rule already prohibits this but is not being consulted at the moment verification logic runs. Add a concrete pre-check: before any verification step, confirm that the verification action itself fits within the declared scope boundary — if it does not, surface the expansion explicitly and wait for approval before proceeding.

The cli-gating hook's 11/13 false-positive rate (blocking read-only operations, grep patterns, commit messages) structurally violates the standing opt-in/non-intrusive design philosophy recorded in memory. Hook precision should be held to the same design standard as feature opt-in gates: minimal blast radius, no interference with unrelated operations. The fix (command-token parsing instead of substring matching) is the mechanical equivalent of making a feature opt-in — it scopes the gate to the actual target and does not fire on passing representations.

High orphan session rate and scope-expand-via-verification-justification are plausibly coupled: sessions may be abandoned mid-task when the user discovers the agent has committed out-of-scope side effects without surfacing them. If scope expansions triggered by verification reasoning were surfaced and approved before execution, the user could redirect rather than abort — reducing both orphan rate and S3 atone recurrence. Treat an unplanned mid-session scope expansion as a checkpoint requiring explicit acknowledgement, not a silent continuation.

The 4-hook cluster root cause (guards matching quoted arg content instead of token position) IS a verification-of-wrong-surface instance at the tooling layer — the guard is checking the human-readable string rather than what the parser actually tokenizes. When fixing any hook in this cluster, frame the fix explicitly as 'check the structural signal, not the content representation,' mirroring the downstream-contract rule from atone: verify what the consumer (the shell parser) sees, not what the author wrote.

Stale graduation proposals pointing at already-shipped rules are the proposals system's own stale-caller-after-rename problem: the rule was 'renamed' (graduated and shipped), but the proposal record was never updated to reflect the new state. Apply the same checklist used for rename sweeps — after any rule ships, grep open proposals for that rule's slug and close or retarget them in the same change, not as a separate cleanup.

Four separate hook proposals sharing one undiagnosed root cause is review-missed-stale-caller-after-rename at the tooling level: the structural insight (token-position, not content) was understood in the first proposal but never propagated to the three sibling hooks. When the fix lands on any one hook, immediately run a grep across all hook scripts for the quoted-arg-content pattern before closing — treat it as a rename sweep, not a point fix.

An unactioned scripts-reliability proposal is a decaying prerequisite in slow motion. Any session handoff or /core-dump that invokes those scripts should explicitly flag them as 'known-unreliable, open proposal pending since 2026-07-13' rather than assuming them stable — the same obligation that triggered handoff-without-naming-decaying-prereqs applies here, just on a longer decay curve.

Two open proposals for the same slug are structurally analogous to a strawman test: acting on either one individually can produce a false sense of closure while the real requirement stays unaddressed. Merge them before action — a split proposal, like a split test, lets any implementation satisfy one half while the underlying invariant remains unguarded.

Three converging dream proposals flag the same post-compaction authorization gap that the S3 atone slug embodies. The CLAUDE.md rule 'treat all approvals as NOT yet approved after compaction' exists but is not binding enough — recurring S3 events confirm the gap is live. Draft a concrete mechanical enforcement: a post-compaction hook or sentinel that resets a session-local authorization register, so the rule cannot be absorbed and silently forgotten mid-task.

These are structural inverses of the same temporal-ambiguity failure: the S3 atone slug fires when the agent treats absent re-confirmation as permission to proceed; the affirm event fires when the agent correctly recognizes a deferred item as still load-bearing. Both live on the axis of 'user said nothing — is that permission or not?' The CLAUDE.md Tier-0 rule for the affirm case should explicitly name the temporal axis: deferral is not cancellation, and absent re-confirmation is not renewed permission. One rule surface, two failure directions — merge them.

The S3-recurrence literal-request-over-intent pattern and the pinned persona gap are the same failure at different layers: the skeptical-reviewer persona produces technically-correct findings (fulfilling the literal request) but they are not human-parseable without the code open (violating the intent). Neither sub-agent-outputs nor audience-aware-writing currently binds the persona output contract to human-readable form. Add an explicit output-contract clause to the skeptical-reviewer SKILL.md: each finding must be self-contained — file, line, failure scenario — readable without the diff open. This closes the literal-over-intent gap at the sub-agent design surface.

Both failures treat git working-tree state as known without a live read: the pinned case uses git checkout inside a mutation loop without first stashing, silently destroying work; the atone case treats git status output as decorative rather than a gate before committing shared state. The missing pre-check is identical: verify the working tree before any operation that mutates it. The existing CLAUDE.md git checkout rule ('git status first, stash -u') does not currently bind automated loops — add an explicit note that mutation and batch loops must stash before any branch-altering step, or the rule only fires in interactive sessions.

The memory finding (a global CLAUDE.md directive silently overridden by an env var without the agent surfacing the conflict) and the S3 atone slug are both instances of ambient state bypassing an explicit gate — in one case an env var, in the other conversational silence, but the outcome is the same: a rule requiring an explicit signal is bypassed by something that 'did not say no.' The fix pattern is identical: any gate bypassable by silence or ambient state needs a positive-confirmation path. Surface the env-override conflict to the user the same way a scope-change would be surfaced — one sentence, explicit, then wait.

Memory writes batched at session-end are silently zeroed out when sessions terminate abruptly (orphan turn-state files). Shift to incremental writes — record after each completed milestone — so a crash cannot erase an entire session's memory contribution. The current pattern creates systematic blind spots wherever parallel-session volume is highest.

Parallel sessions firing within seconds of each other have no structural reconciliation channel for scoped directives. This is the exact directive-divergence failure pin-bb documents. Enforce IPC pre-negotiation of task ownership before any parallel dispatch; without it, divergent directive interpretations accumulate silently with no correction path short of human intervention.

Session-end memory entries are derived summaries, not primary evidence — the cheap-proxy trap pin-96 identifies. Agents reading these entries must treat them as an index requiring verification against primary sources (WAL, git log, actual files), never as authoritative facts. Tag each entry's provenance so readers know what to verify before acting on it.

With 76% of sessions in the tmp project, batch-end memory writes are predominantly encoding tmp-context work rather than target-project context. Memory readers should weight tmp-sourced entries lower; writers should tag each entry with its originating project so downstream consumers can filter by relevance rather than treating all memory as equally authoritative.

Session orphans (abrupt termination correlating with high parallel volume) may be causally linked to miscalibrated hooks firing incorrectly on parallel-session teardown paths. Audit hook gates for correct handling of non-interactive and background teardown contexts — a hook that errors on teardown becomes a session-termination vector, compounding the July-14 density spike's crash rate.

Both are measurement proxies that look like gates but are structurally blind to the actual condition they claim to detect — atone's wrong-layer tests can't observe runtime breakage; the tool-count hook can't observe actual context pressure. When designing any verification gate (test, hook, threshold), explicitly name the failure class it must detect, then verify the gate can observe that exact class rather than a correlated proxy that diverges under the conditions that matter most.

Both describe the same declarative-vs-procedural gap from opposite angles: an acknowledged correction (atone) or an acknowledged standing mandate (pinned) does not modify the gate that fires next. Declarative acknowledgment does not bind procedural checks. Treat every standing mandate and in-session correction as a constraint to re-assert at each decision gate — the acknowledgment does not carry forward automatically.

The high orphan/crash rate concentrated in the burst window is structurally equivalent to declared-ready-without-runtime-exercise: the session terminates before the exercise gate runs, but the work was in-flight and implicitly treated as complete. In burst-parallelism scenarios, any orphaned session must be treated as declared-NOT-ready and its verification step re-queued rather than assumed to have completed.

The tool-count hook appears calibrated to single-session cadence; under burst parallelism, tool counts accumulate faster per session, making the hook fire earlier and with higher false-positive rates. The doomerism threshold miscalibrates proportionally with concurrent session count. Add a per-session token-percentage guard or recalibrate the tool-count threshold to account for burst conditions.

Both substitute a fast-to-generate assumption for a cheap-to-perform check: infra-before-grep assumes absence without a tree search; the context alarm assumes pressure without reading token percentage. The shared meta-pattern is skipping a trivially cheap verification in favor of an assumption that feels adequate. Whenever a gate or guard fires on a proxy signal, ask whether the actual signal is one cheap read away — if so, perform the read.

The S2 advisory-saturation slug says 'advisory exhaustion = hook readiness.' The proposals domain has the mirror case: a hook that already exists but has 3 independent false-fire reports converging on one recalibration. Evaluate both signals in the same review pass — a slug needing a new hook and a hook needing a tuned threshold are the same class of work. When the hook-readiness signal fires for a slug, grep proposals for any existing hook covering the same pattern before filing a 'create hook' proposal; the action may be 'recalibrate' not 'create.'

file-referenced-without-full-path has fired 3× in 3 sessions and exhausted the advisory tier — it needs a mechanical gate. The proposals graduation batch shows ~7 entries where the target rule already exists in rules/. Risk: when this slug's graduation proposal gets filed, it may be miscategorized as 'add a rule' when the correct action is 'escalate existing rule to a hook.' Before filing the graduation proposal, grep rules/ and the proposals backlog for existing coverage of full-path output requirements; the missing piece is the enforcement layer, not the rule itself.

Both are stale-cached-identity failures: familiarity normalization (agent's internal model of 'I know this working directory' overrides the output-time rule) and alias staleness (IPC identity registered at session start becomes stale after restart without a re-registration gate). The fix shape is identical in both domains: re-read ground truth at the consumption point, not at the write point. When designing alias refresh logic for claude-ipc restarts, apply the same 're-validate before trusting' discipline that cache-externally-mutated-state enforces on agent state reads — the cached alias is just as likely to be wrong as a cached file path.

Orphan turn state (a session started a turn and never finished — the write happened, the read never came) and the advisory-channel failure for file-referenced-without-full-path (TL;DR injected at session start, behavior unchanged by session end) share the same structural failure: write-side success treated as delivery confirmation. Neither has a reader-side acknowledgment gate. Both need a consumption signal, not more writes. For the slug: a mechanical stop hook is the acknowledgment gate. For IPC orphan turns: a TTL-based drain that closes incomplete turns and notifies the parent session rather than accumulating silently.

Dead-session mail (32+ messages, up to 7 days old, accumulating in sessions that can no longer receive them) and stale pre-June migration-cleanup proposals (past their target dates, never acted on) are both write-once queues with no expiry, escalation, or drain mechanism. Both give false confidence: the mail looks 'delivered,' the proposals look 'filed.' Neither is actionable by its intended recipient. Treat these as the same architectural gap: any queue that can accumulate items past their actionability window needs either TTL-based expiry or automatic escalation to a live consumer — not just a longer backlog.

These are a confirmed inverse pair: the affirm slug is the successful instantiation of the corrective behaviour the atone slug failed to apply. Graduate them together as a single rule addendum to grep-scope-before-claiming-absence — the affirm instance supplies the positive template ('searched the full design surface before proposing a new one') and the atone S3 supplies the precheck gate ('can I name the surface I searched?'). Co-citing both in one rule prevents the pattern from being treated as two separate lessons.

Both slugs are instances of the same structural failure — a verification gate scoped to a representative subset when the promise requires the full surface. The affirm instance (generated CSS scanned against referencing JS, not just a green CI signal) is the direct corrective template for the atone S3 (uniform feature promise not verified across all exposed surfaces). Merge these into a 'verification-completeness' addendum on exercise-based-verification: before claiming a uniform feature done, enumerate the full surface set, then verify each member — not just the authored artifact.

The pinned domain confirms that the adversarial-reviewer gate (atone-first, adversarial-reviewer before presenting) caught four S2 findings — including a literal-spec deviation — before the owner ever saw them. This is the structural intervention that breaks the verification-undershoots pattern: an adversarial pass is exactly the mechanism that expands scope from 'what I wrote' to 'what the full promise requires.' Graduate the pinned three gates (atone-first, verbatim-ruler, adversarial-reviewer) as mandatory defaults for any uniform-feature delivery, not only owner-reviewed chunks.

The proposals domain has an open core-dump/Resume-Contract cluster (3 proposals, flagged for a batched improvement pass). The atone slug 'repeat-request-dropped-across-sessions' is causally downstream of poor context hand-off — requests that don't survive into the resume contract are invisible to the next session. Treat the core-dump/Resume-Contract batch as the structural fix for the atone pattern: prioritise that cluster over the five cheap-win docs proposals, since improving the resume contract reduces the recurrence rate of the atone slug without any per-instance correction.

The proposals domain shows a hook command-matching flaw independently named in three separate proposals within 48 hours — a classic signal that a fix is being re-proposed rather than landed, which is structurally identical to the atone slug: a replacement (each new proposal) lands without retiring the predecessor (the previous proposal for the same flaw). Before writing the hook fix, grep for all open proposals matching the hook/command-matching keywords, confirm they describe the same root cause, close the duplicates with a single linked commit, and add a one-line 'supersedes prop-N' note — this breaks the re-proposal loop the atone slug predicts.

The cli-gating false-positive on 'render' in commit message bodies is the Nth event in the 9-item hook-false-fire cluster already queued for graduation in proposals. Treat the claude-audit event as the tipping point rather than a new thread: pull the cluster and this event together in one pass, write the shared positional-anchoring helper (match command-as-subject, not command-as-body-substring), and close the graduation. Do not file a new proposal — the root cause is already documented and matured.

Both slugs are instances of the same meta-failure: a rule or correction lands at the specific instance that fired it, not at the class. Comment doctrine exists in rules/comments.md but is not changing behavior across five standing complaints — identical to the morning S2 correction that was scoped to tables/pagination instead of all surface families. Before writing another memory entry about comments, audit whether the existing rule's trigger pattern is narrow enough to fire at the moment the agent is actually writing a comment (a PreToolUse nudge on Edit/Write). If not, the fix is a tighter enforcement surface, not another memory record.

The cli-gating false-positive is a direct instance of partial-sibling-check: the hook audited one form of the surface (does 'render' appear anywhere in the command string) but not the positional sibling (is 'render' the command being invoked vs. appearing in the argument body). When fixing the positional anchor, run a sibling audit across all hooks in the same family — which other hooks scan raw command text without anchoring to argv[0] or the subcommand position? Fixing one without sweeping the family is the exact recurrence pattern the S3 documents.

The pinned insight proposes an 'end-of-window queued-vs-touched diff' to detect accidental slips the /deadline shed ledger cannot see. The sessions domain already produces this signal: isolated sessions with no follow-on activity within 24h are the behavioral proxy for a silently dropped thread. Before building a new tracker inside /deadline, wire the existing burst-and-gap / stuck-task detector as the input signal to the end-of-window audit — the sessions data is the diff the pin is asking to construct.

Atone events that have not graduated to bound rules operate as unbound advice — optional in exactly the way the S3 'prototype-framing' exploit requires. The 23 stale graduation proposals mean 23 known behavioral patterns are still escapable by framing work as a prototype or spike. Processing the graduation backlog is not housekeeping; it directly removes the 'no binding rule yet' escape hatch the S3 event is exploiting. Run one focused graduation pass on the 23 items before the next prototype-framing firing, prioritizing any that touch consistency or sibling-sweep behavior.

The triple-filed guard-dev-server-port bug and duplicate dream git-push proposals are almost certainly artifacts of parallel Agent fan-outs: multiple sessions opening within seconds each independently file the same proposal before any sibling can deduplicate. Before merging the duplicates manually, audit whether they share parent session timestamps in the burst windows. Then add a content-hash dedup gate to the proposal-filing path — hashing on body, not timestamp — or the next burst window will re-accumulate them.

The systemic hook text-matching root cause spanning 4 open proposals is plausibly bidirectional with the burst windows: a misfiring hook may be triggering spurious Agent fan-outs (explaining the burst fingerprint), while those bursts each independently report the same hook bug (explaining the 4 near-identical proposals). Test this by applying the named fix proposal already in the backlog and observing whether burst session density in the next morning window drops. If both metrics move together, the hook fix closes 4 proposals and reduces session inflation simultaneously.

The 23-item atone-graduation queue piling up since Jul 11 likely reflects the Jul-19/20 burst windows: parallel sessions hitting the same failure patterns each file an independent atone event, inflating the queue with structurally identical entries. Work the queue by clustering on failure-class first rather than item-by-item — burst-sourced duplicates will cluster tightly and the true unique count is probably well under 23. This reframes the queue from a 23-item drag to a handful of distinct patterns needing one graduation each.

The Jul-9 orphan session flushing a week late into the current delta is mechanically identical to the April/May stale proposals with blown target dates: both are deferred-work artifacts spawned during parallel sessions that the parent never waited on. Triage them in the same pass — pull the unread orphan mail and the stale proposals together, check whether they reference the same parent burst sessions, and close both tracks at once. Separate triage of structurally identical artifacts wastes two passes.

An orphan session flushing a week late can inject atone or proposal events with stale context into the current queue, making the 23-item graduation backlog appear more urgent than it is. Before working that queue, filter by event creation timestamp and flag anything created before Jul 11 that arrived after Jul 18 — those entries may reference already-resolved patterns and should be staleness-audited before graduation rather than treated as live findings.

The file-referenced-without-full-path pattern has recurred 3× in ~1 month with no mechanical guard landed yet, while the proposals domain shows a 7-proposal cluster pointing at a systemic hook architecture flaw. Before filing another atone event for this slug, check whether any of the 7 hook-architecture proposals in the backlog cover extending filename-dot-stop to catch basename-only path references — if so, escalate that proposal's priority rather than adding a fourth atone entry.

Both slugs are instances of the same root failure: writing output from the agent's internal frame (cwd, file body) rather than the reader's consumption frame (shell context, MEMORY.md quick-scan). The S2 severity on reader-frame-blindness makes this pairing load-bearing. When saving any memory update that changes status (retired, superseded, blocked), treat the MEMORY.md one-liner as a separate deliverable with its own reader frame — the index scanner never reads the file body.

A migration chain 11+ weeks past its target date combined with a four-session cluster that revisits the same project across Jul 9, Jul 17, and Jul 20 suggests repeated re-entry into a stalled work stream without resolution. On the next session touching that project, surface the stale migration chain explicitly at session start and gate forward work on either completing or formally deferring it — repeated context-switching back to an unresolved migration is a re-edit-thrash signal at the project level.

The near-simultaneous session pairs (1–3 minute gaps) are a multi-agent fan-out signature. The 23 [atone] stub proposals filed in a single batch likely originated from one such fan-out pass. Before acting on any of those 23 stubs, verify which already have corresponding rules/hooks in place — a fan-out agent writing proposals cannot see what the main agent implemented in the same burst, producing proposals for already-closed gaps.

A kanban board design gated on decision page D1-D5 was saved during the Jul 20–21 activity burst. High session density immediately after a decision-page gate is a signal that the gate may be blocking forward momentum and sessions are spinning without resolving it. Check whether D1-D5 decisions have been answered; if not, surface the decision page link at the top of the next session touching that design rather than deferring it again.

The systemic hook false-fire bug (reported 3× independently, affecting 12+ hooks) is the most plausible explanation for persona-suggest's 111-fire / 0-heedance signal. Treat that zero-compliance reading as a measurement artifact until the false-fire bug is resolved — calibrating or retiring persona-suggest on this data risks discarding a valid signal. Resolve the false-fire root cause before drawing any conclusions about nudge-style hook compliance rates this week.

Both are the same failure at different layers: 'assumed armed but not wired.' The atone event trusted documentation phrasing to mean the Monitor receiver was active; the memory entries explicitly acknowledge mechanical gates don't exist yet but operate as if intent equals enforcement. Apply the same precheck to every memory-only directive pending mechanical promotion: name the concrete artifact that proves the safeguard is armed — a deployed hook, a passing gate test, an armed listener — before treating it as active.

Both domains surface the same structural gap: enforcement intent is documented but mechanical graduation is backed up. The 23 atone proposals open 12 days that already map to existing rules are the clearest symptom — named the right rule but never closed the loop to a gate. Treat proposal backlog depth as a leading indicator of memory-only fragility: the longer proposals sit unacted, the more load the memory tier carries beyond its design ceiling. Prioritize the atone batch triage before adding further memory-only directives.

The 18-session burst on July 22 averaging ~3 minutes each — consistent with a parallel fan-out or rapid agent-restart loop — likely produced the thin execution history that seeds the adversarial-review gate. If those micro-sessions are the first-run data, the gate calibration risk is not hypothetical but already materialized: seed data from 3-minute agent restarts does not represent normal task distributions. Before the first real adversarial-review run is scored against the gate, verify that burst sessions are excluded from gate training input, or the gate will be tuned to the wrong baseline.

Both are path-legibility failures that have accumulated repeated recurrences without graduating to a single authoritative enforcement surface. file-referenced-without-full-path has 4 atone events and 2 fires this week; filename-dot-stop has 3 near-identical open proposals indicating its existing hook's calibration is unresolved. Consolidate both into one path-legibility gate: basename-only references in output AND trailing-period path syntax are the same reader-friction class. A single scoped hook is easier to calibrate and maintain than two independent nudges with overlapping false-fire exposure.

Before dispatching any sub-agent against a named document, resolve the canonical file path from the live filesystem — not from session shorthand, checkpoint summaries, or board item labels. A shorthand like 'concepts.md CPRD 8.3' is a pointer that can calcify to point at the wrong target; verify the actual path with a Read or rg before treating it as authoritative.

Sub-agent output that makes a factual absence claim ('this file does not exist', 'no such section found') must be independently verified by the main agent before being relayed or acted upon. A sub-agent working from a wrong input document will produce internally consistent but structurally invalid findings — rigorous-looking citations on top of a false premise. Treat sub-agent absence claims as hypotheses, not verdicts.

The proposals domain identifies hooks that pattern-match raw command text rather than command position as a systemic flaw. The same structural shortcut — resolving identity from the nearest-available signal (command text, session shorthand, stale checkpoint) rather than the canonical source — is the root cause of the nearest-authority-substitution atone. When auditing or writing hooks, require position-based or provenance-verified matching; text-pattern matching creates the same false-confidence failure mode that produced the wrong-authority-doc incidents.

The 'verify-authority-before-dispatch' pin and the stale cheap-win proposals share a common execution gap: both represent rules or checks that were recognized but not yet mechanically enforced. Prioritize closing the stale July 13–16 proposals as a batch, since the same delay that let those sit open is the same delay that let 'verify authority' remain advisory rather than a gate — unenforced insights compound into repeated incidents.

Checkpoint and core-dump quality proposals (4 in 8 days in the proposals domain) and the shorthand-calcification pin share the same propagation path: a label written into a checkpoint gets treated as a resolved reference by every subsequent agent that reads it. Core-dump quality improvements should include an explicit rule: document references in checkpoints must include the resolved absolute path, not a human-readable shorthand — so that a resume agent cannot substitute the nearest-sounding file for the intended one.

The two identical design-mocks-never-consulted S3 events in the same atone batch almost certainly originate from the 2026-07-22 fleet burst: parallel agents starting within seconds of each other do not share within-session correction context, so each independently skips the mocks without seeing the prior agent's atone event. The standing session-start reminder fails here by construction — simultaneous spawns all read the same stale reminder before any peer has corrected. The fix must be mechanical and per-agent, not advisory: a PreToolUse gate that blocks writing any named UI element (label, route, component name) until a mocks-read confirmation token is set, firing regardless of what sibling fleet sessions have or haven't done.

The 5 proposals whose rules already shipped are themselves a proxy-surface failure one level up: the proposals backlog is being used as the authoritative surface for 'has this correction been addressed?' when the real authoritative surface is rules/ and hooks/. The proposals system never checked the thing it was supposed to track. Mirror the atone S3 fix here: add a lifecycle step to the proposal-filing flow that checks rules/ and hooks/ before writing any [atone] proposal, and batch-close the 5 stale ones immediately with a 'graduated — rule at rules/<name>.md' annotation rather than leaving them as open noise.

The 24 auto-filed batch proposals sitting untriaged for two weeks are the proposals-layer instance of accumulated-familiarity-skips: the filing agent 'knows' the proposals exist and 'knows' they will eventually be processed, so the at-triage-time check never fires — the familiarity with the backlog concept substitutes for actually working through the backlog. The fix mirrors the S3 atone prescription: make triage a mechanical dated task created in the same action that batch-files proposals, not a deferred intention. The task should block the next dream pass from filing more proposals until the prior batch is dispositioned.

The 10-proposal hook cluster and the fleet burst are mutually reinforcing: parallel fleet agents each independently encounter the same raw-command-matching need, find no shared helper, and each files a proposal — so the cluster grows proportionally to fleet density. The 2026-07-22 burst likely added several of the 10. Graduating this cluster to a shared helper is time-sensitive specifically because fleet use is ongoing: every future orchestration run will add more instances until the abstraction exists. Graduate the cluster now rather than waiting for the next weekly triage, and add a 'check this helper first' pointer to the hook-authoring workflow.

The 3 ancient migration proposals past their own target dates are the structural failure case of not arming the receiver at filing time: each was created with a target date but without a concrete execution path (calendar event, task entry, follow-up hook) established in the same action. The filing session ended its turn without arming anything that would fire when the date arrived. Apply the arm-the-receiver pattern to proposal filing itself as a rule: any proposal carrying a target date must spawn a dated calendar entry or Task-tool item in the same filing action — not as a follow-up, in the same turn — or the target date is fictional.

Rapid context-clear-and-restart cycles likely suppress the invariant-graduation checkpoint that would catch parity gaps before implementation begins. When session patterns show repeated short restarts, treat the missing Resume Contract Standing-constraints entry as a red flag: the invariant was probably stated in a compacted turn and never promoted. Before starting any UI rebuild in a fresh session, grep the previous checkpoint for 'stays / unaffected / threading' claims and promote them to tasks immediately.

Parallel sessions working on the same surface create competing implementation momentum — each session picks up from its own checkpoint without seeing what the sibling session already built. This directly enables silent UX drift: session A rebuilds a flow while session B's context still says 'only threading needed.' Enforce a cross-session parity check at session start when claude-ipc peers are live and the CWD matches an active UI project: read the most recent checkpoint's Standing-constraints before writing any component.

The 14-session burst on July 24 coincides with the kanban v3 correction event. High-density burst sessions under time pressure are the exact conditions where parity audits get skipped — each restart inherits task momentum but drops the 'what did v2 have that v3 must keep' constraint. For any project undergoing rapid iterative rebuilds, pin the previous version's feature inventory as a Standing-constraint in the first checkpoint of each new session, not as a task to do later.

Late-night session pairs 38 seconds apart suggest automated triggers or sprint-end cleanup runs — contexts where no human is actively reviewing parity. Automated or unattended sessions must not perform UI rebuilds without a pre-run parity snapshot: if no human reviewer is present, the session should write a parity ledger and halt rather than proceeding with a rebuild that could silently discard accumulated UX.

The 0% heed rate on persona-suggest (33 fires, never acted on) is causally downstream of the contradiction between two dream-derived hook verdicts the proposals domain identified. Agents cannot comply with a signal that conflicts with itself. Fix the contradictory verdicts first; the compliance metric will only move once the signal is coherent — patching the hook or the allowlist in isolation will not change behavior.

The cli-gating false-positive on 'gh run watch' and the three-proposal hook command-matching bug cluster share a single root cause: verb-unaware pattern matching that cannot distinguish read verbs from write verbs in compound commands. Expanding the allowlist per-command is a patch; the three-proposal cluster is asking for the real fix. Commit the sprint to a verb-aware command-matching engine rather than patching individual allowlist entries, or the false-positive rate will compound as new read-verb patterns accumulate.

Both encode the same upstream failure in different registers: the atone S2 event shows decomposition-first output handed to an absent principal, the memory event shows action items buried after process narration. They are the same agent reflex (mechanism chosen before reader modeled) manifesting in two output surfaces. Because the memory event already has a taxonomy label and a pointer to audience-aware-writing, use it as the graduation anchor and promote to a cross-project standing rule with the atone S2 case as the motivating incident in the rule body.

The atone pattern (decomposition produces an artifact that looks complete but requires further translation before an absent principal can act on it) is precisely the failure the decision-ledger memory corrects. The memory rule ('structure output around what the user needs to DO') is the precheck that would have prevented the atone event. Wire the memory rule as an explicit gate in any agent that produces an artifact for a principal who is not present to resolve ambiguity inline — the check should fire before the artifact is written, not after it is handed over.

Guard-speculative-export fires 9 times with 0 heeded, meaning the agent builds exports before any load-bearing caller exists — the same mechanism-first reflex the S2 atone event documents at the output-surface level. The guard's current framing prohibits the export; reframe its fire message around the caller perspective ('who will read this export and when?') rather than the prohibition, mirroring the reader-model repair the atone event prescribes. A prohibition-framed nudge produces 0 compliance; a reader-framed question may move the metric.

The S3 atone and the pinned boundary-crossing cluster are the same failure at different layers — one in prose register, one in path resolution. Both fire at the moment an internal artifact crosses an audience boundary. Unify them as a single 'resolution-context failure' class: before any output crosses a boundary (reply, handoff, file write), ask 'can the reader verify this without my working context?' for both prose and for every path or evidence citation. A single hook or pre-send gate that checks both prose register and path absoluteness will close both simultaneously.

Three independent observation streams — three near-duplicate hook proposals, an S3 atone for internal-context paths leaking into external replies, and a pinned incident documenting the exact fix (expand to absolute at boundary) — all converged on the same unimplemented mechanical fix. This convergence means the diagnosis is settled but the gate is absent. Consolidate the duplicate proposals into one, tie it to the atone slug, and build the single hook that expands relative paths to absolute at every cross-boundary write. Do not file a fourth duplicate.

The CLAUDE.md growth rate is not only a maintenance problem — it is a gate-bypass risk amplifier.
